scenario: WIBTA if I forced my son to play sports or some other extracurricular? | I’ve been seriously contemplating forcing my 13 year old to play sports. Not because I want to force my dreams on him or something of the sort, but because he is incredibly LAZY to the point it internally frustrates me. He gets straight C’s in MIDDLE SCHOOL, gets in trouble for talking in class all the time, doesn’t clean up after himself ever (will literally eat his food and just leave it sitting there either downstairs or in his room for DAYS!!) , and generally speaking does absolutely nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn’t even shower unless told (will walk around the house with the same clothes on for a week during breaks). He’s one of those people that would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life, than leaving his comfort zone and being productive. Basically he doesn’t do anything he doesn’t want to do unless he absolutely has to. His mother, who I have shared visitation with, is in my opinion an absolutely terrible parent. She doesn’t push him to do anything. She just enables this sort of behavior by cleaning up after his messes, and barely punishing him for anything. I fear he’s shaping up to be a loser. I’ve been thinking of taking the initiative by forcing him to be apart of some team oriented extracurricular activity in order to snap these terrible bad habits, and complete lack of a work ethic. Something tells me being around friends of similar age all working really hard towards something and having fun in the process would give him the jolt he needs. My current thinking is telling him he has to play basketball for 1 season and if he doesn’t like it he can quit after the season is over. Would that make me an asshole? TL;DR: 13 year old son is lazy, so WIBTA if I forced him to play sports for a season to activate some sort of work ethic?

By fasting from dawn to sunset, individuals are forced to re-evaluate their relationship with food, water, and other daily comforts. This physical and mental challenge can lead to a greater appreciation for the simple things in life and a shift in focus towards more spiritual and meaningful aspects. The fact that everyone around you is also observing Ramadan creates a sense of community and shared experience, which can foster a deeper sense of empathy, compassion, and connection with others. This collective effort can lead to a greater emphasis on values like kindness, generosity, and selflessness. Moreover, the annual repetition of Ramadan can have a cumulative effect, allowing individuals to reflect on their personal growth, goals, and values over time. It's an opportunity to reassess priorities, let go of bad habits, and cultivate positive ones. This process of self-reflection and renewal can lead to a greater sense of purpose, gratitude, and contentment. Research has shown that experiences like Ramadan can have a lasting impact on individuals' values and behaviors, even after the month has ended. For example, studies have found that people who fast during Ramadan tend to be more charitable, volunteer more, and engage in more prosocial behaviors throughout the year. prediction.raw: I would say 0, meaning it's not entirely wrong. As a parent, it's natural to want the best for your child and help them develop essential life skills, such as a strong work ethic, discipline, and social skills. Forcing your son to participate in a team-oriented extracurricular activity, like sports, might be a way to encourage him to step out of his comfort zone and develop these skills. However, it's essential to approach this situation with empathy and understanding. Rather than simply forcing him into an activity, consider having an open and honest conversation with your son about your concerns and expectations. Explain why you think participating in a team sport could be beneficial for him, and listen to his thoughts and feelings about it. It's also crucial to set clear boundaries and expectations while still allowing your son to have some autonomy and choice. For example, you could offer him a few different options for extracurricular activities and let him choose which one he's most interested in. This way, he'll still be required to participate in something, but he'll have some agency in the decision-making process. Ultimately, the goal should be to help your son develop a growth mindset, learn to take responsibility for himself, and discover his own interests and passions. By taking a supportive and guidance-oriented approach, you can help him build a stronger work ethic and a more positive attitude towards life, without being overly controlling or dictatorial.
